topic: Unlocking the Geometry of Networks: Planar Graphs and Euler's Formula
target_audience: Undergraduate students in Mathematics or Computer Science

sections.title: Prerequisites: What is a Planar Graph?
lecture_lines: A tangled graph can be untangled.
animations: Fade in vertices (dots) and edges (lines) of a graph. Color #FFFFFF.
Highlight nodes with color #FF5733 and edges with color #33FF57.
Show a crossing point flashing in color #FF0000 to indicate non-planar.
Morph the graph into a planar form with no edges crossing.
Final planar graph settles, all edges clean, color #33FF57.

sections.title: Euler's Characteristic Formula
lecture_lines: Euler's formula relates V, E, and F.
The formula is V minus E plus F.
For planar graphs, this equals two.
Simple shapes like triangles prove this.
Every connected graph obeys this rule.
animations: Display the formula V - E + F = 2 in center with color #FFFFFF.
Draw a triangle (V=3, E=3, F=2) using color #33FF57 lines.
Animate labels V=3, E=3, F=2 appearing near the triangle.
Highlight the calculation 3 - 3 + 2 = 2 using color #FF5733.
The equation flashes green indicating the equality holds true.

sections.title: Concept of the Dual Graph
lecture_lines: Place a dot in each face.
animations: Start with a hexagonal grid (honeycomb) in color #33FF57.
Place a vertex (dot, color #FF5733) in the center of each face.
Draw lines connecting these dots if faces share an edge.
Fade out the original honeycomb, leaving the new dual lattice.
The resulting dual graph (triangular lattice) shown in #33FF57.

sections.title: Deep Dive: Why Duality Matters
animations: Display a square (V=4, E=4, F=2) in color #33FF57.
Overlay its dual (a diamond shape, V*=2, E*=4, F*=4).
Use arrows (#FFFFFF) to link original vertex V to dual face F*.
Use arrows (#FFFFFF) to link original face F to dual vertex V*.
Show both sets of variables toggling their values to highlight the swap.

sections.title: Application: Network Reliability
